UCT and the Skeletons

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
In the early 1920s, on a farm known as Kruisrivier on the Roggeveld escarpment near Sutherland in the Northern Cape, the landowner and his son dug up the skeletal remains of seven individuals, people who had worked the land. The farmer’s son, a medical student donated these individuals bones to the University of Cape Town for their medical school skeletal collection. In the following years he donated two more bodies.

Almost a century later, while doing an archiving audit on the records in the skeletal collection, Dr Victoria Gibbon from UCT’s Division of Clinical Anatomy and Biological Anthropology discovered that a gross injustice had taken place: UCT had unethically obtained the skeletal remains of at least nine individuals, all of whom were San or Khoi.

When Dr Victoria Gibbon was appointed curator of the University of Cape Town’s (UCT) skeletal collection in 2016, she never foresaw that the role would pave the way to one of the most extensive, significant and fulfilling projects of her career. Her first year of curatorship – coincided with important national conversations and initiatives around distinguishing between ethically and unethically obtained human remains within university and museum collections – proved to be a remarkable one indeed.


Further information:
A public apology was made and – through the office of Professor Loretta Feris, Deputy Vice-Chancellor for Transformation – the university initiated a process of restitution and reburial in 2018, starting with the nine individuals from Sutherland.
What would they have been interested.
Gibbon visited the Sutherland community to receive input on the next steps from the Abraham and Stuurman families, who had been identified as descendants of at least two of the individuals in question. “I was quite surprised by the interest from the Sutherland community – the families in particular – in learning more about these individuals,”
“My expectation had been that they wouldn’t want us to study their remains and that they’d want them reburied as soon as possible.”
The nine were revealed as:
• Cornelius Abraham
• Klaas Stuurman
• Voetjie
• Jannetje
• Saartje
• Totje
• Unknown adult
• Unknown younger child
• Unknown older child
Both the Abraham and Stuurman families have descendants who still live in Sutherland, and who have been searching for answers to questions about their family history for decades.
Anthony Mietas, a descendent of Klaas Stuurman, acts as a representative and spokesperson for both families. Mietas said the decision to reveal the two family’s history to the world was so that “broader South Africa will have access to information about who these people were”.
“It was always known to us that indigenous people were around, but given the past, their lived history was not reflected,” Mietas said. “But now we have the scientific proof to say that indigenous people were around in the Karoo, in Sutherland specifically.”

National Geographic ????

With not only the blessing, but also the encouragement of the families for further research to be conducted into the lives and deaths of the nine, Gibbon set to work creating a collaborative project of truly impressive proportions. A truly historical who dunnit.
Areas covered by the team – with members in South Africa, the United Kingdom and Germany – included:

¥ Contextualising the history of the region.

¥ Drawing up an archaeological map of the cemetery.

¥ Biological analyses and reports of these nine individuals.

¥ Computed tomography (CT) scans of each of the skeletons.

¥ 3D facial reconstructions of eight of the nine (the ninth didn’t have a skull present).

¥ Ancient DNA analysis.

¥ Stable isotope analysis, which allows the analysis of diet and migration through one’s lifetime.


Victoria Gibbon: “It’s incredible to be part of something so big, we’ve looked through the literature and can’t find another restitution project that has been so comprehensive in terms of the different types of scientific analysis and the interdisciplinary approach in a project like this.”
She believes that this “internationally precedent-setting” project will also impact on future South African legislation around similar processes.
With the assistance of the students under her supervision, they compiled a biological report on each of the nine individuals.
These reports included crucial information about who they were – how they lived, how they died, whether they were male or female, how tall they were and if there were any signs of trauma or disease.

“This seeking of information from within the community is really what’s special about the project, It’s their search for knowledge and interest in the information.”
Dr Tinashe Mutsvangwa, an expert in medical imaging in the University of Cape Townʼs (UCT) Division of Biomedical Engineering, played only minor role in what has come to be known as the Sutherland Project. Without his expertise, however, the individuals whose skeletal remains were unethically exhumed and donated to the university may forever have remained faceless “A particularly memorable moment of the project for me was being able to show the families a virtual model of one of the individuals.”
This was done with software that is widely used for medical image analysis research. The process involved a careful delineating of the cranium in the CT scan – differentiating it from the background – in order to reconstruct an accurate 3D digital model of each skull.
The 3D models were then sent to Kathryn Smith, a South African visual artist currently completing her PhD in facial reconstruction in the United Kingdom, at Liverpool John Moore’s University’s Face Lab.
In the end, Gibbon said, the original process of restitution, repatriation and reburial has been eclipsed by something much more significant: reinstating a sense of the dignity that was stolen from each of the nine and, by extension, their families.
“This is really about community justice, and for me it’s the most fulfilling project I’ve been involved in, where we give back to community.
Interviews will select from below
Dr Victoria Gibbon – Project leader
Dr Tinashe Mutsvangwa – UCT exoert in medical imaging
Prof Simon Hall- Historical archeologist
Prof Stephan Schiffels From Max Plank DNA Analysis
Kathryn Smith South African in the UK PHD in Forensic Art – facial Reconstruction
Prof Nigel Penn – Historical Studies sketching history.
Prof Judith Sealy Scientific Analysis of Skeleton

Script:


V/O
In the 1920s, on farm just outside Sutherland in the Northern Cape, a farmer and his son dug up the skeletal remains of 7 of their worker’s graves.

Link: The farmer’s son was a medical student at the University of Cape Town and he donated the seven skeletons he found to their skeleton collection…in the following years he donated two more

Link: About 100 years later Dr Victoria Gibbon, whilst doing an archiving audit on UCT’s skeletal collection discovered, this gross injustice, the skeletons had been unethically obtained.

Victoria: At the University human remains are used for teaching and research, mainly for training medical doctors and have come to the university under permit. So what was unique about these 9 it was obvious that they had been removed from a farm from where they had been laid to rest and there was a lot of information about these individuals which is unusual for us.

V/O
Removing bodies from their burial sites is akin to grave robbing and even though this was 100 years later, UCT initiated a process of making amends. The skeletons needed be reburied near their family.

LINK: One of the most important tasks the team had was locating the scene of the crime, the burial sites which had almost disappeared into this harsh, dry landscape.

V/O
It was archaeologist, Prof Simon Hall, who found the burial sites, a few metres away from the families own graveyard,

Victoria: And he saw on the gravestone Dr and so I went into the archives and I found Carl Coetzee was a registered medical student.

V/O
The nine were revealed as, Cornelius Abrahams, Klaas Stuurman, Voetjie, Janetjie, Saartjie, Totjie and three who were unknown.

Anthony: We were always interested in our family tree and Always bothered with family tree and some questions. My mother she informed us about a farm they used to visit at the end of every year, to visit some relatives and that all of a sudden disappeared and they never understood what happened…

V/O
Anthony Mietas is a descendant of Klaas Stuurman, It was in September last year, at a meeting called by UCT that he and the other descendants heard what had taken place.

Claire: What was your reaction?
Anthony: Claire, I think it was a rollercoaster of emotions, it was shock to think that a relative of yours has been lying somewhere for so many years.

Link: Dr Victoria Gibbon came here, to Sutherland, to meet up with families of these nine individuals. It was important that the next steps taken by UCT would be the decision of the families involved.

Victoria: Scared and I was nervous. I actually anticipated anger but what happened was we met these wonderful people who were so curious about knowing more
Claire: What questions were they asking?
Victoria: In particular they were really interested in how they died, who these nine people? So they wanted to know more about the history.

Anthony : Immediately after we started having these conversations amongst our family members, we realized this was much much bigger than the Stuurman and Abrahams family…this is about capturing a history that has never been written in Sutherland we wanted to be able to connect with a face.

V/O
For Anthony’s uncle Alfred Stuurman, it was seeing the disturbed graves that brought it all home.

Alfred: The day when we come here I check out the spot, at first I was shocked it doesn’t even look like a cemetery.
Claire: Were you angry that the remains were just taken?
Alfred: Yes, I was angry, the bones they need respect.

V/O
Back in Cape Town Victoria put a team together to answer the questions the descendants had, ranging from their History, their DNA and what their ancestors actually looked like.

Kathryn: that peaked my interest because not only was it the opportunity to work on eight faces at once, but even more unusual was the knowledge that I had a responsibility to descendant families.

V/O
Visual artist Kathryn Smith, is pursuing a PhD in forensic art at John Moore’s University’s in Liverpool.

Kathryn: You know data sets for Khoisan people don’t exist in the way they do for other population groups, so it involved quiet a lot of research around the subject.

V/O
UCT’s medical imaging specialist, Dr Tinashe Mutsvangwa, was responsible for getting the skeletons in a virtual form…which he would then digitally send to Katherine, in the UK
Tinashe: In order to get this virtual form we had to actually place the skeletal remains in CT machine which works much the same way as X Ray m as an X Ray except it gives you a 3 D rendition of the object you put in. Each one of these skeletal remains st the end of our process was a 3D model which became the template for t he facial reconstruction..

Katherine… He produced the most beautiful 5 D models and shared those with me which I could take straight into our virtual sculpture system

V/O
Reconstructing the facial anatomy, Katherine starts with the muscles …

Kathryn: And then we have a whole set of different future prediction methods that allow us to accurately predict the shape of the nose mouth, the ears get more tricky because we ..ears are biometric so they are like your finger prints.

Kathyrn: We know we are accurate within 2 mm of facial surface for 70% of the whole face but that doesn’t reproduce a relatable face it produces a face model.

V/O
And because this is a facial reconstruction for relatives of the deceased and not for forensic work, relatability is vital.

Kathryn: Although the introduction of emotion in images like this is very controversial, in archeological work like this there is a little bit more freedom because those images have a different job to do.,

V/O
In October this year the `UCT team went to Sutherland to reveal their investigative research.

Kathryn: This was going to be my first encounter with the families, I was anxious but I was also excited but I just hoped they liked them.

Anthony: To be able to put all that data into the face I have a picture of Klaaas Stuurman
Kathryn: There was an immediate response there was an immediate connection, they said they didn’t expect them to look like someone they could meet in the street.

Claire: Here is a man looking back at me
Anthony: Who tells a story on its own and so does the pictures of each of these individuals tell a story.

Alfred: If I look into the photos I see myself, yes, all my family members so Im looking like that one I am looking like the small one.

V/O
Anna de Wee is a descendent of Cornelius Abrahams

Anna: Cornelius Abrahams dis reg.
Anthony: Just by holding up picture Klaas Stuurman, he was one of the them met an untimely death, fortunately the scientist tell it would have been a quick death but the historian tell us it was time when their was a war between and the Khoi and San people…colonialists it’s a sad reflection but a story worth telling.

Victoria: The next step is the re burial we are working to do some kind of memorial it might not be about these 9 people but rather these 9 people have provided a window it will be about lost history or the history that’s not being spoken about. I didn’t intend for this project to take me on a personal journey. We do this work every day but don’t often have opportunity to do what we do every day for the benefit of community.

V/O
And for these descendants it’s an on going journey, knowing that they belong to this area of the Karoo; their children have a place here and their history preserved.

Anthony: We have an opportunity to write History so this is much much bigger and we want to share that to the benefit of our grandchildren to understand where they are coming from, we are talking about a history that was never written up.

Kathryn: You know data sets for Khoisan people don’t exist in the way they do for other population groups, so it involved quiet a lot of research around the subject. V/O UCT’s medical imaging specialist, Dr Tinashe Mutsvangwa, was responsible for getting the skeletons in a virtual form…which he would then digitally send to Katherine, in the UK Tinashe: In order to get this virtual form we had to actually place the skeletal remains in CT machine which works much the same way as X Ray m as an X Ray except it gives you a 3 D rendition of the object you put in. Each one of these skeletal remains st the end of our process was a 3D model which became the template for t he facial reconstruction.. Katherine… He produced the most beautiful 5 D models and shared those with me which I could take straight into our virtual sculpture system V/O Reconstructing the facial anatomy, Katherine starts with the muscles … Kathryn: And then we have a whole set of different future prediction methods that allow us to accurately predict the shape of the nose mouth, the ears get more tricky because we ..ears are biometric so they are like your finger prints. Kathyrn: We know we are accurate within 2 mm of facial surface for 70% of the whole face but that doesn’t reproduce a relatable face it produces a face model. V/O And because this is a facial reconstruction for relatives of the deceased and not for forensic work, relatability is vital. Kathryn: Although the introduction of emotion in images like this is very controversial, in archeological work like this there is a little bit more freedom because those images have a different job to do., V/O In October this year the `UCT team went to Sutherland to reveal their investigative research. Kathryn: This was going to be my first encounter with the families, I was anxious but I was also excited but I just hoped they liked them. Anthony: To be able to put all that data into the face I have a picture of Klaaas Stuurman Kathryn: There was an immediate response there was an immediate connection, they said they didn’t expect them to look like someone they could meet in the street. Claire: Here is a man looking back at me Anthony: Who tells a story on its own and so does the pictures of each of these individuals tell a story. Alfred: If I look into the photos I see myself, yes, all my family members so Im looking like that one I am looking like the small one. V/O Anna de Wee is a descendent of Cornelius Abrahams Anna: Cornelius Abrahams dis reg. Anthony: Just by holding up picture Klaas Stuurman, he was one of the them met an untimely death, fortunately the scientist tell it would have been a quick death but the historian tell us it was time when their was a war between and the Khoi and San people…colonialists it’s a sad reflection but a story worth telling. Victoria: The next step is the re burial we are working to do some kind of memorial it might not be about these 9 people but rather these 9 people have provided a window it will be about lost history or the history that’s not being spoken about. I didn’t intend for this project to take me on a personal journey. We do this work every day but don’t often have opportunity to do what we do every day for the benefit of community. V/O And for these descendants it’s an on going journey, knowing that they belong to this area of the Karoo; their children have a place here and their history preserved. Anthony: We have an opportunity to write History so this is much much bigger and we want to share that to the benefit of our grandchildren to understand where they are coming from, we are talking about a history that was never written up.

metadata.Summary: In the early 1920s, on a farm known as Kruisrivier on the Roggeveld escarpment near Sutherland in the Northern Cape, the landowner and his son dug up the skeletal remains of seven individuals, people who had worked the land. The farmer’s son, a medical student donated these individuals bones to the University of Cape Town for their medical school skeletal collection. In the following years he donated two more bodies. Almost a century later, while doing an archiving audit on the records in the skeletal collection, Dr Victoria Gibbon from UCT’s Division of Clinical Anatomy and Biological Anthropology discovered that a gross injustice had taken place: UCT had unethically obtained the skeletal remains of at least nine individuals, all of whom were San or Khoi. When Dr Victoria Gibbon was appointed curator of the University of Cape Town’s (UCT) skeletal collection in 2016, she never foresaw that the role would pave the way to one of the most extensive, significant and fulfilling projects of her career. Her first year of curatorship – coincided with important national conversations and initiatives around distinguishing between ethically and unethically obtained human remains within university and museum collections – proved to be a remarkable one indeed.
metadata.Further information: A public apology was made and – through the office of Professor Loretta Feris, Deputy Vice-Chancellor for Transformation – the university initiated a process of restitution and reburial in 2018, starting with the nine individuals from Sutherland. What would they have been interested. Gibbon visited the Sutherland community to receive input on the next steps from the Abraham and Stuurman families, who had been identified as descendants of at least two of the individuals in question. “I was quite surprised by the interest from the Sutherland community – the families in particular – in learning more about these individuals,” “My expectation had been that they wouldn’t want us to study their remains and that they’d want them reburied as soon as possible.” The nine were revealed as: • Cornelius Abraham • Klaas Stuurman • Voetjie • Jannetje • Saartje • Totje • Unknown adult • Unknown younger child • Unknown older child Both the Abraham and Stuurman families have descendants who still live in Sutherland, and who have been searching for answers to questions about their family history for decades. Anthony Mietas, a descendent of Klaas Stuurman, acts as a representative and spokesperson for both families. Mietas said the decision to reveal the two family’s history to the world was so that “broader South Africa will have access to information about who these people were”. “It was always known to us that indigenous people were around, but given the past, their lived history was not reflected,” Mietas said. “But now we have the scientific proof to say that indigenous people were around in the Karoo, in Sutherland specifically.” National Geographic ???? With not only the blessing, but also the encouragement of the families for further research to be conducted into the lives and deaths of the nine, Gibbon set to work creating a collaborative project of truly impressive proportions. A truly historical who dunnit. Areas covered by the team – with members in South Africa, the United Kingdom and Germany – included: ¥ Contextualising the history of the region. ¥ Drawing up an archaeological map of the cemetery. ¥ Biological analyses and reports of these nine individuals. ¥ Computed tomography (CT) scans of each of the skeletons. ¥ 3D facial reconstructions of eight of the nine (the ninth didn’t have a skull present). ¥ Ancient DNA analysis. ¥ Stable isotope analysis, which allows the analysis of diet and migration through one’s lifetime. Victoria Gibbon: “It’s incredible to be part of something so big, we’ve looked through the literature and can’t find another restitution project that has been so comprehensive in terms of the different types of scientific analysis and the interdisciplinary approach in a project like this.” She believes that this “internationally precedent-setting” project will also impact on future South African legislation around similar processes. With the assistance of the students under her supervision, they compiled a biological report on each of the nine individuals. These reports included crucial information about who they were – how they lived, how they died, whether they were male or female, how tall they were and if there were any signs of trauma or disease. “This seeking of information from within the community is really what’s special about the project, It’s their search for knowledge and interest in the information.” Dr Tinashe Mutsvangwa, an expert in medical imaging in the University of Cape Townʼs (UCT) Division of Biomedical Engineering, played only minor role in what has come to be known as the Sutherland Project. Without his expertise, however, the individuals whose skeletal remains were unethically exhumed and donated to the university may forever have remained faceless “A particularly memorable moment of the project for me was being able to show the families a virtual model of one of the individuals.” This was done with software that is widely used for medical image analysis research. The process involved a careful delineating of the cranium in the CT scan – differentiating it from the background – in order to reconstruct an accurate 3D digital model of each skull. The 3D models were then sent to Kathryn Smith, a South African visual artist currently completing her PhD in facial reconstruction in the United Kingdom, at Liverpool John Moore’s University’s Face Lab. In the end, Gibbon said, the original process of restitution, repatriation and reburial has been eclipsed by something much more significant: reinstating a sense of the dignity that was stolen from each of the nine and, by extension, their families. “This is really about community justice, and for me it’s the most fulfilling project I’ve been involved in, where we give back to community.
